title: Pow(x, n)
description: Brute force to optimized: multiplying one copy of x at a time versus exponentiation by squaring, then an iterative version with no recursion stack.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a real number x and an integer n, compute x raised to the power n, without using a built-in power function.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Exponentiation by squaring, halving the exponent instead of shrinking it by one, expressible recursively or by walking the exponent's binary representation iteratively."],["Difficulty","Intermediate"],["Tags","Math, Recursion"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing halving beats linear stepping for repeated multiplication, correctly handling negative exponents via reciprocal, and converting the recursive halving solution into an iterative bit-walking version to drop the recursion stack."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a real number x and an integer n, compute x raised to the power n, without using a built-in power function. A negative n means the reciprocal of x raised to the positive version of n.

blocks.title: Analogy: Doubling Your Investment
blocks.text: Picture reinvesting money by doubling it at every step. To reach a target that would normally take many single dollar additions, doubling gets there in far fewer steps: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. Computing x to a large power works the same way, instead of multiplying by x one copy at a time, repeatedly squaring what you already have reaches the answer in far fewer multiplications.

blocks.caption: Halve the exponent and square the result, instead of multiplying one copy at a time

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: x = 2, n = 10

blocks.text: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: 2 to the power -2 is 1 divided by 2 squared, which is 0.25.
Example: x = 2, n = 0
Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 is 1, by definition.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what repeated multiplication is really building.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Multiplying x by itself n times, one copy at a time, does exactly n units of work, no matter how those n copies are grouped together.

Observation 2: x to the power n can also be written as (x to the power n divided by 2) squared, meaning the same final answer can be reached by solving a problem roughly half the size, then just one extra multiplication.

Observation 3: Halving the problem at every step, instead of shrinking it by one, is what turns a linear amount of work into a logarithmic amount, the same idea used in binary search and fast exponentiation generally.

Observation 4: This halving idea can be expressed either as recursion, solve the half, square it, or iteratively by walking through n's binary representation directly, squaring a running value and folding it in wherever a bit of n is set.
That reasoning alone already points past the linear loop, straight at halving the exponent instead of decrementing it.
6. Brute Force Solution
The most direct approach is to multiply x by itself, once for every unit of n, handling a negative exponent by first taking the reciprocal of x.
Step by step algorithm

items: If n is negative, replace x with 1 divided by x, and make n positive.
Start a running result at 1.
Multiply the result by x, n times in a row.
Return the final result.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: multiply in one copy of x at a time, n times total

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The negative exponent case is handled first, converting x to its own reciprocal and n to its positive magnitude, specifically so the rest of the logic only ever needs to deal with a positive exponent.
result starts at 1, not 0, since 1 is the correct answer for n = 0 and also the correct multiplicative identity to start accumulating from.

The loop multiplies result by x exactly n times, in a fixed, unconditional pattern, which is precisely what makes this version take time proportional to n itself rather than to the number of bits in n.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because repeated multiplication by x, exactly n times, is the direct definition of x raised to the power n.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one multiplication per unit of the exponent.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: for a very large exponent, like n close to 2 billion, looping that many times is far too slow. The key insight that unlocks a much faster approach is that x to the power n can be built from x to the power n divided by 2, squared, cutting the remaining work roughly in half at every step instead of by one.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why multiplying one copy at a time works but is slow: for a very large exponent, like n close to 2 billion, looping that many times is far too slow to ever finish in practice.

What repeated multiplication is really building: the same final product, regardless of how the individual multiplications are grouped or ordered.

Can the problem be split in half instead of reduced by one: yes, x to the power n equals x to the power n divided by 2, squared, with one extra multiplication tacked on if n is odd.

What does that buy: solving a problem roughly half the size, then doing a constant amount of extra work, exactly the recurrence that produces logarithmic time.

The core idea: recursively compute half the exponent's result, then square it, adjusting for an odd exponent.

Instead of multiplying by x one copy at a time, compute the result for half the exponent first, then square it. If the exponent is odd, multiply in one extra copy of x after squaring to account for the leftover.
This is exponentiation by squaring, a classic technique for computing large powers efficiently.
9. Optimized Solution
Recursively compute the result for half the exponent. If the exponent is even, square that half result directly. If it is odd, square the half result and multiply in one more copy of the base.
Dry run for x = 2, n = 10

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Exponent","Computation","Result","Why"],"rows":[["fastPower(2, 0)","0","Base case","1","The recursion bottoms out here, anything to the power 0 is 1."],["fastPower(2, 1)","1","1 times 1 times 2","2","Odd exponent: the half result (1) is squared, then one extra copy of the base is multiplied in."],["fastPower(2, 2)","2","2 times 2","4","Even exponent: the half result (2) is simply squared."],["fastPower(2, 5)","5","4 times 4 times 2","32","Odd exponent: the half result (4) is squared, then one extra copy of the base is multiplied in."],["fastPower(2, 10)","10","32 times 32","1024","Even exponent: the half result (32) is simply squared, giving the final answer."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: halve the exponent, square the result, recursively

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because x to the power n and (x to the power n divided by 2) squared are mathematically identical whenever n is even, and squaring the half result while multiplying in one more copy of the base correctly accounts for the leftover factor whenever n is odd. Every recursive call halves the exponent, so the recursion reaches its base case, exponent 0, after only about log base 2 of n calls, rebuilding the full answer on the way back up through a constant number of multiplications per level.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Exponent is even","The half result is squared directly","x to the power n, exactly"],["Exponent is odd","The half result is squared, then one more copy of the base is multiplied in","x to the power n, exactly, accounting for the leftover factor of x"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: fast_power is written as a separate nested helper specifically so the sign handling, taking the reciprocal for a negative n, only needs to happen once, outside the recursive halving logic, which only ever deals with a non-negative exponent.

half is computed by a single recursive call and then reused twice, multiplied by itself, rather than making two separate recursive calls, which is exactly what keeps the number of recursive calls logarithmic instead of doubling at every level.

The even and odd branches both square half first, differing only in whether one extra copy of base gets multiplied in afterward, since an odd exponent always has exactly one leftover factor after halving.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), a genuine complexity class improvement, since the exponent is halved at every recursive call.
Space: O(log n), for the recursive call stack, one frame per halving.
10. Further Optimization: Iterative, No Recursion Stack

The recursive version still uses O(log n) call stack space. The exact same halving idea can be done iteratively instead, walking through the binary representation of n directly: repeatedly square a running product, and fold it into the answer whenever the current bit of n is 1.
Dry run for x = 2, n = 10 (binary 1010)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","n before this step","Lowest bit","result after this step","current after squaring","Why"],"rows":[["1","10","0","1","4","Bit is 0, nothing folds into result; current is squared in preparation for the next, smaller n."],["2","5","1","4","16","Bit is 1, so result folds in the current running power, 1 times 4 equals 4; current is squared again."],["3","2","0","4","256","Bit is 0 again, result stays unchanged; current keeps squaring."],["4","1","1","1024","65536","Bit is 1, folding in the current power, 4 times 256 equals 1024, gives the final answer; the loop ends once n reaches 0 next."]]}

blocks.text: Once n reaches 0, result holds 1024, matching the recursive version exactly.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: walk the bits of n directly, squaring as you go, no recursion needed

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: current_product starts at x itself and is squared once per loop iteration, which is exactly what makes it hold x, then x squared, then x to the 4th, then x to the 8th, doubling its own exponent every single round.

The check for whether n is odd tests exactly the bit of n currently being processed, folding current_product into result only when that bit is set, mirroring how binary numbers are built from powers of two.
Dividing n by 2 each round, using integer division, is what advances to the next bit position, and the loop naturally ends once n reaches 0, having processed every bit of the original exponent.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), the same order as the recursive version.
Space: O(1), a genuine reduction from the O(log n) recursion stack, since the iterative version only tracks a few running values.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is halving the problem instead of shrinking it by one, a technique that shows up constantly whenever repeated multiplication, repeated doubling, or divide and conquer structure is involved. Converting the recursive halving solution into an iterative one that walks the exponent's binary representation directly is a common follow up that removes the recursion stack entirely.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to handle a negative exponent by taking the reciprocal of x before applying the halving logic.
Off by one mistakes in the odd exponent case, forgetting the extra multiplication by the base.
Not considering that n's most negative possible value cannot always be negated safely in a fixed width integer type, a wider type avoids this.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Always returns 1 regardless of x, the base case of the halving recursion and the natural starting value of the iterative result."],["Negative n","Requires taking the reciprocal of x and negating n before applying the same halving process either way."],["x = 0 with a positive n","Correctly returns 0, since multiplying any number of zeros together, however they are grouped, always gives 0."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This is one of the most classic demonstrations of divide and conquer thinking applied to arithmetic. Moving from the naive O(n) loop, to the recursive O(log n) halving solution, to the iterative bit walking version, mirrors exactly the kind of layered optimization interviewers want to see walked through out loud.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid n multiplications", think: exponentiation by squaring, halve the exponent instead of subtracting one.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the recursion stack", think: walk the exponent's binary representation iteratively, squaring a running value and folding it in on set bits.
If the interviewer says "what about a negative exponent", think: take the reciprocal of the base first, then apply the same halving logic to the positive exponent.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does halving the exponent produce logarithmic time instead of linear time?
Can you convert the recursive halving solution into an iterative one without looking at the answer first?
How would you handle an exponent so large it does not fit in a normal integer type?
What changes if x itself is a matrix instead of a real number, computing a matrix power?
Can you compute x to the power n modulo some other number m efficiently, without ever computing the full, possibly enormous, result?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Fast exponentiation in modular arithmetic, computing x to the power n modulo m, which reuses this exact same halving technique, just adding a modulo after each multiplication.

Matrix exponentiation, which applies the identical halving idea to matrix multiplication instead of scalar multiplication, useful for computing large Fibonacci numbers or other linear recurrences quickly.
Binary search and other halve-the-problem-instead-of-shrinking-it-by-one techniques, which share the same underlying logarithmic time reasoning.
Bit manipulation problems that walk an exponent or index bit by bit, the same iterative pattern used in this problem's further optimized version.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force loop runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. Exponentiation by squaring brings time down to O(log n), a genuine complexity class improvement, first with O(log n) space for the recursive version, then down to O(1) space with the iterative bit walking version.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: exponentiation by squaring, halving the exponent instead of shrinking it by one, expressible either recursively or iteratively.
Core Idea: x to the power n equals (x to the power n divided by 2) squared, with one extra multiplication if n is odd, letting the exponent be halved at every step instead of decremented by one.
Time: O(n) for the brute force, O(log n) for both the recursive and iterative optimized versions.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(log n) for the recursive version's call stack, O(1) for the iterative version.

Most Important Observation: halving a problem at every step instead of shrinking it by a fixed amount is what turns linear work into logarithmic work, a pattern far more general than just this one problem.

Interview Difficulty: easy to write the naive loop; recognizing exponentiation by squaring, and then converting it to an iterative form, is what demonstrates real command of divide and conquer thinking.
One line memory trick: square the half, and fold in one extra factor whenever the exponent is odd.
